51.0.0.en: 1- Have mercy upon me, O God, according to thy lovingkindness: according unto the multitude of thy tender mercies blot out my transgressions.

51.0.1.en: 1- David felt that his two sins, adultery and murder, deserved death, and he no longer had any chance of escape from divine justice except by asking for the mercies and compassions of God. By this David humbly declares his weakness and his sins.

51.0.2.en: 2- David's repentance for his two sins mentioned before drove him to repent of all his sins, and to ask God's forgiveness. His insistence in asking for divine mercy declares his faith in God's love and in His ability to forgive all sins; indeed, this shows that David looked by the spirit of prophecy to Christ who would come in the fullness of time to take away all sins from the penitent and those who believe in Him.

51.1.0.en: 2- Wash me throughly from mine iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin.

51.1.1.en: 1- David expresses his evils with three words: the first, transgressions (v. 1), which in the original Hebrew means a turning aside from God; iniquity (v. 2), which means the justification of faults; and sin (v. 3), which means the evil intention accompanying the deeds. Therefore for the remedy he used three words: blotting out for the transgressions, washing for the iniquities, and cleansing for the sins.

51.1.2.en: 2- Because David feels that his faults are many, he asked for a thorough washing of his iniquities. And this washing is accomplished by the following:

51.1.3.en: a- Trials, that a person may keep away from sin and hate it.

51.1.4.en: b- The blood of Christ the Redeemer, which David saw by the spirit of prophecy to be partaking of the Holy Sacraments, which forgive and strengthen a person against sin.

51.1.6.en: 3- The washing refers to the water of Baptism, which purifies the baptized from his sins.

51.2.0.en: 3- For I acknowledge my transgressions: and my sin is ever before me.

51.2.1.en: David confesses his transgressions, and by this he receives forgiveness for them. His sin he set always before his eyes, to offer repentance for it at all times. And when he did this God helped him by sending Nathan to him and pricking his conscience, that is, the feelings of remorse increased within him, for he truly deserves the mercies of God.

51.3.0.en: 4- Against thee, thee only, have I sinned, and done this evil in thy sight: that thou mightest be justified when thou speakest, and be clear when thou judgest.

51.3.1.en: Be clear when thou judgest: to be just, upright and praised in Your judgment.

51.3.2.en: 1- David feels that his sin is directed against God before it is directed against a man, because God is his Creator, and He is the one who holds him to account if he does not walk uprightly. And even if those around him flatter him and praise him because he is king, he does not forget that God is the one who will judge him. Here David affirms his confession of his sin and does not justify himself, but shows the enormity of his sin, because he did it with contempt and defiance in the sight of God. Consequently there is nothing before him but repentance to receive the mercies of God.

51.3.3.en: 2- David's confession of his sin shows the justice of God, and that He is clear in His judgment. For when God punishes David, David deserves it, and it is not injustice. And if God forgives him, this is a great mercy from Him which David does not deserve. God's gifts are many, for He raised David from shepherding sheep and made him king, and taught him His commandments; but David sinned, and consequently deserves divine justice and punishment. David is a sinner and God is righteous and true in His promises.

51.4.0.en: 5- Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me.

51.4.1.en: 1- David was raised with a godly mother who was a servant of God (Ps 116:16); he does not mean that he was born of adultery, but he means the ancestral sin with which all men are born, when he mentioned the iniquity and sin in which he was born.

51.4.2.en: 2- David's mention of his being born in sin shows his humility and contrition before God, and consequently draws out the compassionate mercies of God, who has pity on those who plead to Him. By this verse David lives in the contrition of repentance and abasement before God, and at the same time enjoys God's tenderness and forgiveness, as God makes an excuse for him because he was born in sin and is exposed to falling into it.

51.5.0.en: 6- Behold, thou desirest truth in the inward parts: and in the hidden part thou shalt make me to know wisdom.

51.5.1.en: The hidden part: the secret place.

51.5.2.en: 1- David feels the love of God, who was pleased that the inward being of David, and his innermost parts, incline to truth and good, and not to doing evil, and that the sin into which he fell was a plot of Satan; that is, David feels that God loves him and makes an excuse for him.

51.5.3.en: 2- David also feels the kindness of God, who did not rebuke him before the people for his sin, but sent to him in secret ("the hidden part") Nathan the prophet, and made his sin known to him, so David declared his repentance, and Nathan told him that God had forgiven it.

51.5.4.en: 3- David by the spirit of prophecy saw the Truth, who is the Word of God, the Second Hypostasis, that is, Christ, in whom the Father was well pleased, and he also perceived in secret, that is, between himself and his own soul, that Christ is the true Wisdom, and he knew of the Incarnation and its mysteries, which would be accomplished in the fullness of time, and would give him and all believing mankind true salvation, purity and cleanness, unlike the Mosaic law, which was practiced in the days of David, for it is all a type of Christ who would come in the fullness of time to forgive his sins.

51.6.0.en: 7- Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean: wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.

51.6.1.en: Hyssop: a wild plant with a long stem having dense leaves at its end, like palm fronds. In ancient times they used it to clean their bodies of dirt and sweat. The Jews put vinegar on it and lifted it up to Christ on the Cross to drink (Jn 19:29).

51.6.2.en: 1- David asked God to cleanse him with hyssop, which was used for purification according to the law of Moses (Num 19:6, 18; Lev 14:6). This shows David's sense of the multitude of his sins, and on the other hand his trust in God who is able to cleanse him whatever his sins.

51.6.3.en: 2- The Jews used hyssop to smear the lintel and the two side posts of the door with blood, that the destroying angel might pass over them (Ex 12:22). So hyssop is a type of Baptism, since it is used for washing away dirt and for purification, and at the same time the blood put on it is a type of the blood of Christ, which cleanses from every sin. David longs for purification in all its dimensions, whether in the Old Testament or when it is perfected in the New Testament.

51.6.4.en: 3- David longs to be washed by the hand of God, so that he becomes pure, dazzling white like snow, and this expresses his faith and hope in the new, pure life in which he wants to live after God forgives his sins.

51.7.0.en: 8- Make me to hear joy and gladness; that the bones which thou hast broken may rejoice.

51.7.1.en: 1- Although sin disturbed and grieved David, the grace of God, His love and His forgiveness restore his peace to him, and even gladden his heart, because his joy rests on his sense of God's presence.

51.7.2.en: 2- God broke David's bones, because when David fell he remembered the fear of God, so he repented greatly and felt the guilt of his sin. But God's tenderness did not leave him in his sorrows, but restored his gladness to him when he repented. Sin produces sorrow, but joy is of the fruits of the Holy Spirit, whom God gives to His penitent children.

51.8.0.en: 9- Hide thy face from my sins, and blot out all mine iniquities.

51.8.1.en: 1- As David feels the enormity of his sin, he asks God to hide His face from his sins, that is, to forget them, and look upon David with an eye of compassion, and restore to him his sonship.

51.8.2.en: 2- When David fell into the two sins of adultery and murder, he awoke and repented of these two sins, and since his remorse was intense he examined himself concerning all his former sins, and offered remorse for all of them, and hoped of God that He would blot them out and forgive them, that he might become completely pure; for if David were to keep one sin without repentance, he would lose the Kingdom.

51.8.3.en: Take care to offer repentance for every sin, that you may receive the forgiveness of God; for if you try to hide it and cover it and do not confess it, God will judge you for it, but if you repent He will forgive it for you and hide His face from it, and you will live in joy on earth, and then in heaven.

51.9.0.en: 10- Create in me a clean heart, O God; and renew a right spirit within me.

51.9.1.en: 1- After David's fall he felt that his thoughts and feelings had all been defiled, and therefore he needed new, pure feelings, so he asked God to create in him a heart that desires life with God.

51.9.2.en: 2- David also asked for the renewal of his spirit, by which he means his conscience and all that God distinguished him with as a human being from the rest of creation. And he asked for a right spirit that has no aim but the love of God, so that his innermost parts become longing for God and lead his body on the way to the Kingdom.

51.10.0.en: 11- Cast me not away from thy presence; and take not thy holy spirit from me.

51.10.1.en: 1- David lived enjoying fellowship with God from the time he was a boy shepherding sheep, and he used to seek God in every tribulation, and He rescued him and supported him, as when he killed the lion and the bear, and afterward Goliath, and then hundreds of the Philistine enemies. But after his fall he was sure that he was not worthy to enjoy seeing God, yet when he repented the longings for fellowship with God were renewed within him, so he implored Him not to cast him away from His presence, because seeing God and fellowship with Him is life for David.

51.10.2.en: 2- The Spirit of God who dwelt in David and gave him prophecy, and also the wisdom to lead the kingdom as king, the strength for war and victory, and the wisdom to apply justice in judgment, David was no longer worthy of enjoying all this because of his falling into sin. But he is still a king, a military commander and a judge, and indeed as a spiritual man he needs the Spirit of God who guides him, and pricks him if he errs, and gives him gifts and abilities that he necessarily needs; therefore he implored God not to take His Holy Spirit from him.

51.11.0.en: 12- Restore unto me the joy of thy salvation; and uphold me with thy free spirit.

51.11.1.en: Free spirit: a spirit obedient by free will.

51.11.2.en: 1- Sin produced sorrow in David's heart, and he lost all the feelings of joy he had lived with God, so as he repents he implores God to restore to him the gladness and joy of salvation from sin, that he may live with Him anew.

51.11.3.en: 2- By the spirit of prophecy David sees that complete salvation is accomplished by the redemption of Christ, and this salvation is able to fill the heart of man with joy, so David longs that man regain his joys which he lived in the garden of Eden by receiving the salvation of Christ.

51.11.4.en: 3- David also asks God to uphold him by renewing his spirit, that it may be obedient to the commandments of God, and so go forth in freedom and its own will, resting on the grace of God, to enjoy being with Him.

51.12.0.en: 13- Then will I teach transgressors thy ways; and sinners shall be converted unto thee.

51.12.1.en: 1- Since David tasted the bitterness of sin and repented, he longed to warn all who had fallen into sin, that they may repent like him and enjoy peace in the hands of God. And as he caused others to stumble by his sin, now he calls every one who has fallen into sin to repent; for he who has experienced the bitterness of sin and repented is the person most able to call others to repentance.

51.12.2.en: 2- The sinners and transgressors whom David means are all his senses and faculties which were defiled by sin, so as he repents he teaches and trains his thoughts, senses, body and all his faculties not to turn aside from God, but to keep His commandments and walk in His ways.

51.12.3.en: When you fall into sin do not be content with sorrow or settle into despair, but rise quickly in hope, and ask humbly before God that He have mercy on you and forgive you, and even support you by His power to make up for all you missed, and by this the devil will not gloat over you, and God will rejoice in your repentance.

51.13.0.en: 14- Deliver me from bloodguiltiness, O God, thou God of my salvation: and my tongue shall sing aloud of thy righteousness. 15- O Lord, open thou my lips; and my mouth shall shew forth thy praise.

51.13.1.en: 1- David asks God to remove from him the effects of his sin, which are the blood of Uriah the Hittite whom he killed, and the blood of all who were killed with him from the army. By bloods he also means all who were made to stumble by David, the first of them the wife of Uriah the Hittite, and everyone who knew David's sin and stumbled at him. He asks that God forgive him all these bloods, because he trusts that God loves him, so he calls Him "God of my salvation," that is, the one who cares for me and is concerned for my salvation from every sin. So with faith and great hope, and by the spirit of prophecy, he sees Christ, the true Savior in the fullness of time, who saves him and saves mankind from its sins.

51.13.2.en: 2- When David is purified from sin, and God forgives him its effects, he can praise God the righteous, the holy, who justified him and forgave him his sins. So he stands before God and utters words of praise and glorification, which confirm his faith and fill his heart with peace.

51.13.3.en: 3- Sin closes man's heart to God, and also shuts his mouth, but repentance returns man to his natural state, and he enjoys the grace of God, which opens his lips, so he sets out in praise, thanking God who received him and forgave him. For God is the mover of the feelings and words of praise in His children and those who love Him.

51.14.0.en: 16- For thou desirest not sacrifice; else would I give it: thou delightest not in burnt offering. 17- The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.

51.14.1.en: 1- Although David was committed to the law and to offering sacrifices, such as the sin offering and the trespass offering which a person offers if he errs, he makes clear here that the offering of sacrifices is not sufficient, not only because they are a type of the sacrifice of Christ, but because God stipulates that they be accompanied by a humble, penitent heart. If the solution were to offer sacrifices, David would have offered many of them, especially since he is a king and able financially to do so, but he declares clearly that this alone does not please God, but He stipulates a spirit that is contrite in repentance. The meaning of this is that God despises sacrifices not accompanied by true repentance, but rejoices in the humility of the hearts of the penitent.

51.14.2.en: 2- The greatness of humility lies in its being a sacrifice of dignity, a sacrifice of man's own will, and a readiness to endure insults, and God greatly rejoices in humble hearts. Humility was perfected in Christ, who was crushed on the Cross and in the sufferings for our redemption; here the good pleasure of the Father is perfected.

51.14.3.en: I ask You, Lord, to keep me from causing others to stumble, lest I be called to account for their blood. And give me, Lord, humility to keep Your commandments and to accept sufferings for Your sake, and then You will keep me in Your right hand from every evil, and fill my heart with peace and joy.

51.15.0.en: 18- Do good in thy good pleasure unto Zion: build thou the walls of Jerusalem.

51.15.1.en: Zion: the most important of the five mountains on which the city of Jerusalem is built. The name Zion is used in many places to denote the city of Jerusalem.

51.15.2.en: 1- After David tasted the sweetness of God's forgiveness of him, he asked Him to bless Jerusalem with His good pleasure toward her, and to build her walls, that is, that she become a strong, fortified city. This shows the extent of David's love for the holy city Jerusalem, and the dwelling of God in it. He feels his membership with the people of God, and asks on behalf of all the believers who worship God in this holy city.

51.15.3.en: 2- By Zion and Jerusalem David also means himself, that is, he asks God to bless him and fortify him against the attacks of the devil, that he may remain in the love of God, and that God may show His kindness and good pleasure in His incarnation for the redemption of mankind. By Jerusalem he also means the Church of the New Testament, and the walls are the Apostles, who kept the faith and preached it to the whole world.

51.16.0.en: 19- Then shalt thou be pleased with the sacrifices of righteousness, with burnt offering and whole burnt offering: then shall they offer bullocks upon thine altar.

51.16.1.en: 1- When God blesses Jerusalem, His holy city, and all the believers who come to her, these believers rejoice and are encouraged, and offer to God sacrifices of righteousness and perfect offerings, that is, the feelings of their hearts, their thoughts, hymns of praise going forth from their mouths, and works of righteousness that bear witness to God, so that He is glorified in them.

51.16.2.en: 2- After hearts are moved on the way of the love of righteousness, the sacrifices become acceptable "bullocks," and even please God, because they proceed from hearts filled with love for Him.

51.16.3.en: 3- David sees by the spirit of prophecy the Church of the New Testament, which, after enjoying the redemption of Christ, the believers in her offer sacrifices of righteousness and the perfect offerings of their hearts; indeed their tongues meditate on the praise of God, and their works glorify Him, and in the end they offer bullocks, which are the giving of their lives in spiritual striving and service, and then it is completed in martyrdom.

51.16.4.en: Express your love for God, who blesses you every day with many blessings, by offering the sacrifices of your lips, which are your prayers and hymns, and then complete them with works of mercy and service, out of your love for your Redeemer who gave His life for you.

51.16.5.en: The conduct of the wicked and the righteous. To the chief musician. A psalm of David the prophet, when Doeg the Edomite came and told Saul, and said unto him, David is come to the house of Ahimelech: "Why boastest thou thyself in mischief, O mighty man?") ... v. 1) Introduction:

51.16.6.en: 1- Its writer: David the prophet, as appears from the title of the psalm.

51.16.8.en: At the beginning of David's flight from the face of Saul, after David went to Ahimelech the high priest in the city of Nob, in which the priests lived, where he ate the showbread and took the sword of Goliath, and Doeg the Edomite saw him there, and told Saul, and stirred him up against Ahimelech, so Saul killed Ahimelech and all the priests, and only one of them escaped, Abiathar (1 Sam 21).

51.16.9.en: 3- Doeg the Edomite was of the descendants of Esau and joined the Jewish people, and rose to be the chief of the herdsmen responsible for the flocks of Saul, and he is a wicked man, inclined to shedding blood, so he carried news to Saul, which were facts, but supported by provocations to Saul, and all of it lies, as he showed Ahimelech cooperating with David against Saul, and this did not happen. And when Saul ordered the killing of the priests, all the servants of Saul were afraid of that, so Doeg came forward and slew them all with the sword; Doeg is wicked, and boasts in evil; therefore he is a type of the Antichrist, the opponent of the truth.

51.16.10.en: 4- This psalm shows that the power of the wicked, however overbearing it may seem, is quick to pass away, and nothing awaits the wicked but divine punishment. But the righteous God blesses and rewards, and this establishes the believers in the life of righteousness.

51.16.11.en: 5- This psalm is considered one of the eight psalms whose title states that David was driven out and fleeing from the face of Saul, and they are called "the psalms of the fugitive," and they are (Ps 7, 34, 49, 52, 54, 56, 57, 142).

51.16.12.en: 6- This psalm is not found in the Agpeya.
